definition: Bayesian Optimization is sequential black-box optimization for expensive evaluations. It fits a probabilistic surrogate to observed configurations and costs, then uses an acquisition function to choose the next configuration, balancing exploration and exploitation.
intuition: Use a model of what is known about the objective to decide which unknown experiment is worth running next.
mathematical_foundation:
$$
x_t = \arg\max_{x \in \mathcal{X}} a(x; \mathcal{D}_{t-1})
$$

The surrogate models the unknown objective from observations `\mathcal{D}_{t-1}`; acquisition function `a` selects the next expensive evaluation.
advantages: Acquisition functions expose the exploration-exploitation trade-off.
Supports noisy objectives and mixed search spaces through suitable surrogates.
Uses prior observations, so it can be efficient when evaluations are expensive.
limitations: A misleading surrogate or noisy validation signal can direct trials to the wrong region.
Sequential decisions limit parallel throughput unless batch methods are used.
Surrogate and acquisition quality can degrade in very high-dimensional or highly conditional spaces.
